title: The Passing of Glyn Powell and the Enduring Legacy of Suzanne Capper
text:
A former ringleader of a sadistic gang that tortured teenager Suzanne Capper to death has died, prompting her family to launch a charity in her honor.
The news that Glyn Powell has passed away from cancer has brought back harrowing memories of one of the most sadistic crimes in British history.
Powell was a central figure in a twisted group that kidnapped and tortured sixteen-year-old Suzanne Capper in 1992. The brutality of the assault spanned seven days in Moston, Manchester, where Suzanne was held captive in conditions that can only be described as demonic. At the time, Powell was twenty-nine years old and acted as one of the ringleaders alongside his estranged wife, Jean, and an accomplice named Bernadette McNeilly.
During her captivity, Suzanne was subjected to unthinkable cruelty, including being tied to an upturned bed, having her head and pubic hair shaved, being beaten with belts and wooden implements, and having her teeth extracted with pliers. The horror culminated when the group doused her in petrol and set her ablaze, singing a cruel song as they left her for dead.
Despite the extremity of her injuries, Suzanne survived long enough to provide police with the names of those who had tortured her, ensuring that her attackers faced the justice system and received life sentences. For Stephen Capper, Suzanne's younger brother, the death of Powell is a small piece of closure in a lifelong battle with grief and trauma.
Now forty-six years old, Stephen reflects on the absolute evil of the perpetrators who manipulated his sister and treated her like a slave. The psychological scars left by the event are profound; Stephen suffers from PTSD and is frequently triggered by smells that remind him of the burns unit at Withington Hospital. He recalls the haunting stench of charred flesh and the sight of his sister, who was unrecognizable due to the severe burns.
He describes a nervous habit of biting his nails and flicking the clippings into an ashtray, where the smell of burning nail clippings triggered by a cigarette butt takes him straight back to the hospital ward in December 1992. His anger is compounded by the fact that all the killers, including the ringleaders Jean Powell and Bernadette McNeilly, have been released from prison.
For Stephen, the passing of Glyn Powell is simply one less monster on the planet, but his fight to ensure that the perpetrators are held accountable continues. Beyond the horror of her death, Stephen is determined to remind the world of who Suzanne Capper actually was as a person.
Contrary to the narratives that sometimes painted her as a troubled youth or a street urchin, Suzanne was a kind, funny, and loving sister who acted as a babysitter and best friend to Stephen. The family had enjoyed a normal, happy childhood with vacations to Torquay and a father who worked hard as a taxi driver, until the family dynamic shifted following his parents' separation.
To preserve this memory and turn a tragedy into a force for good, Stephen and a childhood friend, Samantha Dale, are launching a charity called Lost Voices. This initiative, along with the publication of their book titled The Lost Voice: Remembering Suzanne Capper, aims to transform Suzanne's story into a catalyst for positive change to help others in need.
The event to launch the charity is scheduled to take place at FC United in Moston, poignantly located just a short distance from the site where the atrocities occurred. Through these efforts, they hope that Suzanne's legacy will not be forgotten and that her voice will finally be heard in a way that brings light to such a dark chapter of history
